prompt: In the lab, `They were charged twice for order 4471.` is seven words and eight tokens. Where does the eighth come from?
hint: Look at the end of the sentence.

choices.text: The number 4471 is split into two tokens
choices.why: In the lab a run of digits is one token.

choices.text: The full stop
choices.why: Right: every punctuation mark is a token of its own in the lab.

choices.text: The newline that `echo` adds at the end of the line
choices.why: Whitespace is not counted by the lab's tokenizer.

choices.text: The word *charged*, which is long enough to be split
choices.why: The lab never splits a word; a real tokenizer might.

prompt: Put inside one JSON field, `{"summary": "…"}`, the eight-token sentence came to how many tokens?
hint: The second `pl tokens` line.

prompt: The reply to `t01` is 32 tokens and its summary is 8 of them. What are the other 24?
hint: Count what is around the sentence.

choices.text: The spaces and line breaks of the indented JSON
choices.why: The lab does not count whitespace at all.

choices.text: The message, which the model repeats before answering
choices.why: The reply holds no copy of the message.

choices.text: Field names, labels and punctuation
choices.why: Right: 19 punctuation marks and 5 names and labels.

choices.text: Hidden reasoning
choices.why: The stand-in writes nothing it does not print.

prompt: Does the lab's token count tell you what a provider will bill for the same text?
hint: Whose tokenizer does a provider bill by?

choices.text: Yes, because every tokenizer counts punctuation the same way
choices.why: Real tokenizers often merge punctuation with what sits beside it.

choices.text: No: the provider counts with its own tokenizer
choices.why: Right. What carries over is the proportion of structure, not the number.

choices.text: Yes, for English text
choices.why: Language does not make two tokenizers agree.

choices.text: Only for JSON
choices.why: Format does not make them agree either.

prompt: A cap chosen by thinking about how long the ___ ought to be comes out too small, because that part is only a quarter of the reply.
hint: The part of the reply a person reads.

prompt: With `max_tokens=30`, how many of the forty replies passed every check?
hint: The `all` line of `pl check runs/cap30.jsonl`.

prompt: Why did `t35` pass under the cap of 30 when 39 others failed?
hint: Look at `out` on its last line.

choices.text: Its message asked for a short answer
choices.why: It did not; the customer just loves the shop.

choices.text: The stand-in noticed the cap and wrote less
choices.why: Nothing in the reply changed; the cap removes, it does not plan.

choices.text: Its reply was 29 tokens
choices.why: Right: its summary was four words, and the whole reply fitted under the cap.

choices.text: The cap does not apply to replies sorted as other, since nothing reads them
choices.why: The cap applies to every reply alike.

prompt: A reply ends with `stop: max_tokens`. What does that tell you?
hint: Compare it with `stop: end`.

choices.text: The limit ended it, not the model
choices.why: Right, so the end of the reply is missing.

choices.text: The model judged the answer complete and stopped
choices.why: That is `end`.

choices.text: The prompt was too long for the model to read
choices.why: The cap is on output, not input.

choices.text: The reply cost more than the cap allows
choices.why: The cap counts tokens, and a cut reply is charged for what it wrote.

prompt: A colleague sets `max_tokens` to 20 on a prompt that writes one-paragraph replies to customers, to keep them short. What will the replies look like?
hint: Does the cap change what the model plans to write?

choices.text: Shorter and complete: the model fits its answer to the limit
choices.why: The limit decides where writing stops, not what is written.

choices.text: Unchanged, because the provider ignores very small limits
choices.why: A limit is applied whatever its size.

choices.text: Rejected before any text is written
choices.why: Nothing refuses the request; it is cut.

choices.text: Most of them stopped in mid-sentence
choices.why: Right. To get short replies, ask for them in the prompt.

prompt: Under `v4-words.txt`, `t37` came back shorter and still valid JSON, while the cap of 30 broke it. What is the difference?
hint: Which of the two changed what was written?

choices.text: The words prompt also raised the cap, so the reply had room to finish
choices.why: No cap was set in that run.

choices.text: The request changed what was written; the cap removed the end
choices.why: Right: asking shapes the answer, the cap only cuts it.

choices.text: A request for length turns the cap off
choices.why: Under the cap of 30 the words prompt failed 39 times as well.

choices.text: Short summaries are never cut
choices.why: They are, when the frame plus the summary passes the cap.

prompt: Mean output tokens went from 38.0 to 36.8 when the prompt asked for under 12 words. By how many tokens per reply did the mean fall?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: Why did asking for a summary under 12 words lower the mean output by so little?
hint: Which part of the reply is allowed to shrink?

choices.text: The stand-in ignored the request and wrote its usual one-sentence summaries anyway
choices.why: It obeyed: `t37` was cut to twelve words.

choices.text: The prompt grew by a few words, and the length of the output follows the prompt
choices.why: Input length does not set output length.

choices.text: Only the summary shrinks, and the JSON frame around it stays the same size
choices.why: Right, and many summaries were under twelve words already.

choices.text: Twelve words is the stand-in's minimum
choices.why: It has no minimum; `t35`'s summary was four words.

prompt: Under `max_tokens=30`, the prompt asking for under 12 words still passed 1 reply in 40. What should change?
hint: Twelve words of summary sit inside a frame.

choices.text: Ask for fewer words, under six
choices.why: That fights the cap with the content; the cap is what is wrong.

choices.text: The cap: well above the asked length plus the frame
choices.why: Right. The request sets the size; the cap is only the guard.

choices.text: Drop the request, since the cap already limits length
choices.why: Then every long reply is cut instead of shortened.

choices.text: Parse the cut replies leniently
choices.why: A cut reply is a failure, not a parsing problem.

prompt: Which of these are true of asking for a length in the prompt? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare it with the cap.

choices.text: It changes what the model writes
choices.why: Yes: the brace still closes.

choices.text: It has to be checked, like a label
choices.why: Yes: the stand-in kept twelve words where under 12 allowed eleven.

choices.text: It makes the cap unnecessary
choices.why: The cap is for the reply that ignores the request.

choices.text: It does not stop a reply that ignores it
choices.why: Yes, which is why the cap stays.

prompt: Where does choosing a cap start?
hint: A cap must stay out of the way of ordinary replies.

choices.text: The length you asked the summary to be
choices.why: The summary is a quarter of the reply.

choices.text: The provider's largest allowed value
choices.why: That guards against nothing.

choices.text: The mean output of a run, since most replies are close to it
choices.why: Half the replies are longer than a mean-ish cap.

choices.text: The longest ordinary reply, measured over a test set
choices.why: Right: `pl latency` prints it.

prompt: With the confidence field added and a cap of 100, how many tokens was the longest reply?
hint: The last line of `pl latency runs/v9-100.jsonl`.

prompt: Under a cap of 50, two replies with the confidence field were cut, yet `all` read 36, as it did with a cap of 100. Why?
hint: What else was wrong with `t37` and `t24`?

choices.text: Both were already failing on a label
choices.why: Right: the cut changed why they failed and not how many failed.

choices.text: The harness leaves cut replies out of the count
choices.why: They are counted, as `json` failures.

choices.text: The harness ran the two cut replies again without the cap
choices.why: Nothing is re-run; each call is made once.

choices.text: A cut reply passes `all` if its category is right
choices.why: A reply that fails `json` fails every check after it.

prompt: A reader adds the missing closing brace to `t24`, parses it, and gets the right answer. Why is that still a bad rule for the reader?
hint: Where will the next cut land?

choices.text: Adding a character to a reply is slower than parsing it
choices.why: Speed is not the problem.

choices.text: The next cut lands inside a summary, and the repair accepts it with its end missing
choices.why: Right: a reply that stopped at `max_tokens` is a failure, whatever is left of it.

choices.text: JSON forbids adding braces after the fact
choices.why: Nothing in JSON forbids it; the risk is accepting a truncated answer.

choices.text: The confidence value would be lost
choices.why: In `t24` it was there; the trouble is the other cuts.

prompt: Put the steps of setting a cap in order.
hint: Measure, set, watch, repeat.
items: Run the prompt over a test set and read the longest reply
Set the cap well above that, about twice
Treat every reply that stopped at the cap as a failure, and count them
Measure again when the prompt changes

prompt: Match each command to what it told you in this lesson.
hint: One each.

pairs.right: How many tokens a piece of text is
The mean and the longest output of a run
One reply and why it stopped

right_distractors: The price of a million calls

prompt: After a prompt change, `pl check` starts reporting `json` failures with the reason `cut off at max_tokens`. What do you do?
hint: The prompt changed and the cap did not.

choices.text: Add *be brief* to the prompt so that the replies fit under the cap again
choices.why: That changes the answer to suit a guard that is in the wrong place.

choices.text: Close the cut replies in the reader, adding the quote and brace they are missing
choices.why: A cut reply is a failure, not something to repair.

choices.text: Measure the new longest reply and raise the cap well above it
choices.why: Right: the cap was set for the old prompt.

choices.text: Set the temperature to 0
choices.why: Temperature does not decide where writing stops.
